utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber understood that the parties would have agreed to resolve the scheduling problems of this week by skipping Witness Misic and after Mr. Pajic to hear the evidence of Mr. Simic only, and I urged the parties to take care that we'll be able to finish at quarter past 2.00 this Friday sharp, because we have no possibility to extend that session. So try to agree among yourselves that not only examination-in-chief and cross-examination but also re-examination that there's sufficient time that you organise yourself in that way. And the Chamber might need, not much as matters stand now, but might need some time for oral decisions as well and that will, as we can foresee now, take not more than 15 minutes, but that should be calculated as well. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. It just will take a brief moment, but I will have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We left off yesterday talking about the two radio relay communication routs from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps. Now, in relation to the protected encrypted route via the FM-200, can you tell us how encryption and transmission of voice communications would happen? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This other radio relay, 074, that worked with Vlasenica -- I mean, in order to have this kind of communication, we needed two FM-200s. We needed crypto encryption on both sides, KZU-71, and a telephone multi-channel device with a time redistribution of channels that was called IMD-310. The speech information provided, or written text, in order for it to be relayed to the other side, this speech would be turned into a binary system by way of impulse code modulation. It was transferred -- [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] For this kind of signal to be transmitted, an AMD-310 is needed. This speech signal would be turned into an impulse code or delta modulation with a time distribution of channels. So in order to transmit this kind of signal, we needed impulse code modulation at a speed of 256 kilobyte per second, 512, 1.024 kilobyte per second, all depending on the channels on that protected route. Usually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please slow down, otherwise we'll not be able to receive your full evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this speed was applied depending on the number of channels. Was it eight or more? 32 was the maximum. Such a signal, binary-modulated, the code impulses were protected through KZU-71, and then it goes to a 690 to 960 megahertz range, and then it goes through antennae to the other side, and then it is modulated on the other side, demodulated, depending on whether it is eight or 32 channels. So such a signal is impossible to be listened into. It is fully protected. Say, if it is 10 kilometres, as was the case with the Drina Corps, so it is 10 kilometres as the crow flies, usually the power was not very big, the output. 09074 from 93, that is to say, this radio relay route 09074 and then 9658, was digital or, rather, full protection of speech was guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, while being transmitted via the radio relay device on a particular frequency channel, how would that impulse signal sound to the human ear of a listener on the same channel but without all the equipment that you described?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These signals that enter the frequency-carrying device or this telephone have a permanent tone, usually. So the speech cannot be understood. Nothing. Whereas telegraph signal goes in interpreted impulse. Again, it's some kind of tone but it's interrupted, the impulses are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now could you just describe for us briefly how that tone signal is made understandable and rendered to normal speech on the other end, the recipient's end of a radio relay communication?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This tone signal is sent to the other side, and the other side, or rather the relay station, also has the same FM-200. So this radio relay device that has a certain megahertz range and it has KZU-71 and a multi-channel device for time distribution of channels in impulse code modulation; that is to say, on this KZU-71, the deciphering or -- no, demodulation takes place, and then through this multi-channel device, a redistribution of signals is carried out in the receiver or rather in the so-called channel section. So every one of them has eight channels and then it is turned into speech information. So in the AND itself, this transformation takes place into speech information and as such it is sent to the cable itself as speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how much further Mr. Ivetic would like to go on this particular topic, but just to be clear, it's the Prosecution's position, and it has been the evidence of the Prosecution in this case, that the intercept operators did not have the capabilities of intercepting FM-200s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that help, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It doesn't change matters in terms of understanding the technology and as I'm about to now go to the RRU-800 and the differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But to understand the technology is mainly important if there's dispute about what could be done by whom with that technology. If that there's no disagreement that there could be no intercepts, we don't have to understand -- then we don't have to understand what the technology of the system is which could not be intercepted. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My recollection is that there were two different witnesses talking about the FM-200, one of which said they could not and one, speaking for different entity, said that they could. That's my recollection anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we've heard it. You are moving --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the RRU-800 anyhow, so therefore time enough to find out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, how about voice communications via the unencrypted radio relay device RRU-800 from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps? How would a voice communication be processed and transmitted by this radio relay device?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just recall that FM-200 had a protected and unprotected mode of operation, may I just add that. And this other thing or rather this other combination, the RRU-800 0607, how speech was transmitted. Speech was transmitted as opposed to protected information. Different devices were used, RRU --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness would have to clearly state all the devices. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I just -- it was -- would have one been one of my questions, what you told us about the two modes, the protected and the unprotected mode, does that mean that you could activate the protection and you could switch it off, to say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? This device does have this possibility to work digitally and in analogue manner, but the telephones themselves are different. When there is this protected version, then a multi-channel device is used, 310, and I'm referring to telephones. Now, when there is unprotected communication, it is 12K --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for FM-200 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 12K what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12K communication. That's what it was called. It was not used for the unprotected system for analogue communication. So let me explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we don't have to hear necessarily all the technical details. If we need, we'll ask questions about it or the parties will do so. But I do now understand that whether or not the protected mode was used or not depended on other devices that were used, whether they were such that the protection could work but perhaps the more old fashioned ones did not fit into this protection system. And apart from that, if you would use devices which were fit for this protection system, could it still be activated or non-activated or would it automatically be activated if the right equipment was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for protected systems, the equipment that I listed is automatically used in protection. In order to move onto a different system of work in the same device, FM-200, on the device itself there is a system, and we can choose whether we want to work in an unprotected or protected mode. Let me emphasise that when the regiment is analogue, unprotected, again certain channels can be individually protected - not the entire system necessarily, 12 channels, 24 channels. So even with an unprotected system in 12K, channels could individually be used with a different kind of KZU; for instance, usually KZU-71 and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the operator would decide whether he would not -- that individual channel to be protected, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, depending on the importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the importance of the communication whether it had to be protected or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you had started answering my question about how a voice communication is processed and transmitted by an RRU-800 and -- if I could just find it. If you could -- if could you finish that, I think you had -- that's where you mention the 12K and had left off and had answered the Judge's questions. Could you please explain for us how voice communications are processed and transmitted by a RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other route towards the Drina Corps, 0607, worked through RRU-800, and the multi-channel telephone device was an RM4A. Speech or written information that enters that channel is modulated in terms of frequency in a range from 03 to 108 kilohertz, and then such a signal is modulated and is transmitted to the radio relay device 610 to 960 megahertz. By way of an antenna it is sent out. Then on the other side, that is received, this signal, through electromagnetic waves. It is demodulated, it is brought down to the MF signal, and in the telephone system on the other side there can be 12K or another device --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear which one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on one side there can be RM4 but not necessarily, not necessarily the same telephone on both sides. I don't know if I'm being clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in addition to the 12K another device which the interpreters did not hear. Can you tell us which other device apart from a 12K?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The multi-channel telephone device RM4A. Just like 12K, it can have 12 or 24 channels depending on what is needed. These two devices can operate mutually because there is no problem involved as they have the same frequency range.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, while the signal is being transmitted between the devices, how would that signal sound to the human ear of someone on the same frequency channel but without this equipment?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These speech signals are modulated within a certain frequency, so there is no other written information or speech. There is just certain tones that enter the frequency-carrying devices, and then as electromagnetic waves they are being transmitted. So it's just the signal, the tone signal, the interrupted signal, that is there, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can --

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, we need equipment to demodulate that signal, to turn it into a low frequency signal so that it would go to a certain kilohertz range and to be transmitted into speech on the other side. So along the route there is no other speech that functions. There is no speech that can be heard, just some kind of interrupted tone. However, in order to have proper quality of sound, the speech signal has to be strong enough in terms of decibel. A certain value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let's try to keep matters short. Do I understand your answer to be that it would not be recognizable as speech if you would listen to it? Because that's the issue. I think I heard you say "da," but you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the essence of that is that no speech is transmitted along the relay route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the human ear would receive no speech. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, returning to the two routes, the RRU-800 and the FM-200 going from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps, which -- what would each route be most frequently used for? What type of communications?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I didn't understand. The interpretation came late, so I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the FM-200 route and the RRU-800 route going from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps, for what would each route be most often used? What type of communications?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A digital route, the protected one, was mostly used for direct communication between the commander of the Main Staff, the commander of the Drina Corps, operative centres of the Drina Corps, of the Main Staff, the telephone switchboards of the Main Staff and the Drina Corps, and the automatic telephone number that was forwarded was 332. And the radio relay route 0607, the analogue route, which did not have protection was used for other communications, most frequently for the transmission of telegraph signals; that is, to send written information that was processed at the encryption station. Because such information could not be listened into along the route, they could not be decrypted along the route without the appropriate KZU devices. Also a three-digit automatic number was used along a protected route. It all depended on the importance of secure communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, what communications hub was utilized by the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka and the G-1, or Goljak, site for radio relay communications?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio relay hub Veliki Zep was used for radio relay communication between the Drina Corps and the Main Staff. These radio relay devices located at Veliki Zep, they were connected with the devices of -- that carried frequency by a cable, VF, towards the V-1 installation, and the distance is 1 kilometre or 1 and a half kilometre, I forgot. So telephone devices were at the G-1 and radio relay devices were at the radio relay hub Veliki Zep, and they were connected between them by a special cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of special cable was this that connected G-1 with Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a normal high frequency coaxial cable for underground communications, wire communications, and it had 24 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat 24 what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other cable was a smaller cable with a smaller cross-section, 0.8, and the previous one was 1.2. So these are the cables usually used for underground wire communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What portion of the 1 and a half kilometres link was underground?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I waited for you to have it clarified, what the witness referred to when he mentioned 24. Witness, you said: "It was a normal high frequency coaxial cable, I take it, for underground communications, wire communications, and it had 24..." 24 what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kilohertz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sorry, sorry. 24 pairs of wires. We call them pairs. Couplings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How much of the 1-and-a-half-kilometre link of that wire was underground?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire cable, from Veliki Zep to the Bijeljina feature was under the ground. The whole length.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you're recorded as saying the entire cable from Veliki Zep to the Bijeljina feature. Is that what you intended, the Bijeljina feature?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I said from Veliki Zep up to G-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now what can you tell us about the frequencies used by the VRS to transmit via radio relay devices? Did they change during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of communications of the Main Staff of the VRS had a frequency plan for all radio relay hubs of the Army of Republika Srpska. This frequency plan, nobody could change it without his orders. Nobody could modify it without his approval. This frequency plan programmed regular annual changes of frequency. However, since we had two important radio relay hubs in the territory of Yugoslavia, stationary hubs, Cer and Strazbenica, this was not practiced. In order to change frequencies at these two radio relay communications, approval was necessary from the chief of communications of Yugoslavia, and for other hubs the approval of the chief of communications of the Army of Republika Srpska. So from 1992 until 1995, under this annual plan there were no changes of frequency. I don't know why. It was the chief of communication's decision. I was an operator; I was supposed only to service these communications. We changed frequencies at given moments when we had interference, when some new radio relay routes were introduced, but it was only by 2 to 5 megahertz. We would modify communication -- we would modify frequency by a very small amount if there was interference. So this frequency plan stipulated the same frequencies from 1992 to 1995, except for a few situations that I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question for clarification. You said nobody could change it without the orders of the chief of communications of the Main Staff. It was not allowed to change without his permission or was it technically not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was technically possible, but without his orders nobody was allowed to change it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First, to follow-up on your answer, sir, you said in cases of interference we could modify the frequency to a small degree, 2 to 5 megahertz up or down. Would that be in the transmission or in the receiving end of radio relay transmissions?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on which frequency was closer, what was the frequency of a device close to you. The receiving end or the transmitting end. There had to be an appropriate distance between frequencies, up to 20 megahertz. Frequencies could not be reduced lower than that. The distance between frequencies could not be smaller. The difference had to be at least 27 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But where would you go up -- on what end would you tune-up or down to 2 to 5 megahertz to better hear the signal? How would that be accomplished?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these 2 to 5 megahertz, you could do it at the transmission device or the receiving device. The transmitter would tune-up by 2 or 5 and the receiving end also. They had to do it simultaneously. The -- the receiving end had to set their frequency at the same value as the transmission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now to follow up on the Judge's question, could a single operator on the system on their own change the frequency and still maintain communications with the rest of the network; that is to say, change the frequency from that on the communications plan for the radio relay network?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be done, but it wasn't done. As far as I know, nobody did it. But technically, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if someone wanted to intercept and listen in on transmissions sent via an RRU-800 or an FM-200 radio relay device, where would they physically need to be located?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to eavesdrop on radio relay communications, the training we received at school was this: The intercepting side had to enter the beam of electromagnetic waves between two radio relay devices that were operating, and they were usually set, as I said, at a distance of up to 50 kilometres with clear optical visibility. And on this route, the signal noise ratio had to be very sharp in order for modulated communication to function well. So with two radio relay devices, the other side would have to have also two radio relay devices and be located up to 25 kilometres from either end and have an appropriate frequency-carrying device, and then they could listen in to unprotected analogue communications. Or they could set two stations close to both of these, like a couple of kilometres behind the receiving end and a couple of kilometres behind the transmitting end. If they had only one device, they could hear only one side. To listen in to the entire conversation, a radio relay device had to be set halfway between the two or behind the radio relay devices, both of them. And then, of course, they had to tune into the correct frequency. Radio relay centres were always located behind the lines. If the enemy wanted to listen in, the enemy had to go very deep into our territory in both versions; if they wanted to set their station halfway between the two, or two of them behind each.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard some evidence and has been told by the Prosecution that it is possible for both sides of a conversation to be transmitted via one channel of a radio relay device by way of leakage of the sound from the speaker in the handset to the microphone in the same handset of one participant in the conversation. What are your technical observations as to this proposition?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the speech signal coming out of the receiver, it's very small, very few decibels, so that signal could not be carried further. I mean, on these devices carrying frequency and relay devices, it doesn't have enough power, that signal, not enough value in decibels in order to enter the frequency modulated and received on the route as a wave. In the contrary case, I mean, the signal of that kind of power cannot be transmitted. That's what I learned at school at least. It has to have a power of 160 to 183 decibels. That's why radio relay routes were set at a distance of not less than -- not more than 50 kilometres. All other conversations cannot be carried far enough. They -- you can't hear it. The audibility is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in terms of personnel operating radio relay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification here. I have some difficulties in understanding your answer because you are referring to values, which I'm unable at this moment to link to the question and to what was said. The question was about incoming signals which would be made audible and that through that audible incoming sound, that that would leak into the microphone which would give the signal in the other direction. Now, I have some difficulties, because if the person who receives the signal and receives it as sound audible for him, that is either, I would think, could be detected by the microphone, and you could -- even if it's not strong enough, you would even be able to amplify it because you need to hear it anyhow. The human ear would need to be able to hear it. Why, then, a microphone, which is next to or close to the human ear could not receive that same sound and it would be included in sending it the other direction? I have difficulties in linking your answer to what the question was. First of all, is it clear to you what my understanding was of leakage, which was used by Mr. Ivetic as an expression? That's my first question. Is it clear to you what I -- how I understood it and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Coming out from the headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the headset, of course, could be anything. You can open it, you can close it, you could -- headsets are just incoming sound. I do not understand your reference to the 160 to 183 decibels because that's a huge sound, isn't it? You almost become deaf if you listen at 160 decibels. It would even perhaps harm your ears. So I do not understand how to link your information with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone and the headset are connected electrically between them. And this sound leaking through the headset is of a very small value. That's what I spoke about already. And, as such, it enters the device very weakly. It has to have enough power in order to be modulated inside the radio relay device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you for a second. Is there any chance that you're talking about electric leakage, whereas perhaps the question was about sound leakage? You understand what I mean? And I that I think that you're talking about a kind of electromagnetic leakage, whereas I think the evidence the Chamber heard was about sound, that is audible sound, leakage, leaking into the microphone. But I may have misunderstood it, and I would appreciate the assistance of the parties if I show that I've misunderstood it. Could you answer the question, whether you're talking about electromagnetic leakage, and whereas the question may have been about sound, that's, audible sound, leakage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that the microphone and the headset are electrically connected. I understood you. The headset transmits the signal into an understandable speech signal. I was not talking about electromagnetics. The sounds signal enters the headset, but it's so weak that it cannot enter the device on the opposite side. It's too weak. It cannot be transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say the volume would not be good enough to leave the headset and enter the microphone in any useful way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also tell us when you refer to 160 to 180 decibels, what exactly were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the power of the signal that is modulated and put out along the route. That's the necessary power of the signal for the signal to be modulated and transmitted onto the route. So a signal has to have a certain required power to be transmitted along the route. And this speech leaking into the headset, it depends all on the device, if the device is too far away and cannot be received and transmitted onto the route. It has to be strong enough, otherwise it would not be understandable and could not be transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as I understand, decibel is a unit for volume power, more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for induction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're talking about 160 decibels, what kind of volume are we talking about? Is that whispering or is that a siren? Because you use those values.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not a siren. Normal speech, when you talk into the microphone. It can be measured, so that's why we have this range for reducing the signal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say normal conversations, normal speech is approximately at 160 decibels. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not speech but the signal that enters the radio relay device. That's the required power for the signal to enter. I'm not talking about speech. The device itself will evaluate how strong the signal is. If it's too weak, the device cannot transmit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it needs 160 decibels to receive it in a useful way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the value the signal has to have in order to be transmitted. That's the value of the modulated signal putting -- put out into the route. It's not the power of our speech. The signal enters the device, then it is frequency-modulated in the device-carrying frequency, and the signal, modulated in such a way, needs to have the power of 160 to 183 decibels to be successfully transmitted. I'm talking about the required power of the signal, not the volume of the speech. And if we're talking about normal speech, the device itself will decide if the signal is strong enough or not, if it can enter the range of the modulated signal in order to be successfully transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, most likely my understanding of what a decibel is is too limited to fully understand. But it is approximately time for a break, Mr. Ivetic. Would you want to use this last minute to clarify the matters forever or would you rather take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it's safer for everyone to have the break and come back with fresh minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you've been warned sufficiently enough. You're excluded from this hearing after the break. We'll take a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to briefly address the present situation, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Mladic is removed from the courtroom for the duration of the testimony of the present witness. We do not know for sure whether the next witness will start giving his evidence today or only tomorrow. Mr. Mladic has an opportunity to follow the proceedings through videolink from where he is now. If Mr. Mladic would decide to go back to the Detention Unit, that will be understood by the Chamber as a waiver to be present during the beginning of the testimony of the next witness if that next witness would start giving testimony today. You can explain this to Mr. Mladic if you wish, but that is how the Chamber understands the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just now, we talked to General Mladic. We conveyed this information to him, and he said to us that in that case he would stay here and follow via videolink, and then if Simic starts today, he would like to be in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, you will understand there's no guarantee that Mr. Simic would start his -- by the way it is -- yes, it is Mr. Simic will start his testimony today. We do not know. That's -- but you have fully understood, then, the situation; Mr. Mladic as well. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, if the parties -- I was a bit confused by the decibels, as you may have noticed. Most likely explanation is that decibel is not only used in acoustics but also in electronics. If that is the case, if the parties would agree on that, that would at least make clear what type of confusion is possible there. Not to say that the whole leakage issue, whether this is the explanation or not is a totally different matter. It's just a matter about concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of the personnel operating the radio relay device communications system at the Main Staff of the VRS in 1995, what can you tell us about their overall level of skill and training?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The personnel operating the communications equipment - that is to say, all the devices in the communication system of the Army of Republika Srpska - were mainly professional military personnel; that is to say, officers who had completed military schools and also civilians serving in the army who had completed certain schools in the field of electrical engineering so that they could operate such equipment. So the personnel were professionals who were capable of operating this kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would to take a look at 65 ter number 24516 with you in e-court. Now, first of all, sir, do you recognise this drawing or sketch that is on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this sketch or drawing is depicting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can we get an English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that there is only a B/C/S copy of this Prosecution 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe for us what this sketch depicts?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a sketch that I drew of the underground part of the facility; that is to say, the distribution of rooms underground in G-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this sketch accurately depict the distribution of spaces or rooms in the underground G-1 object, or are there need for any corrections?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sketch is mainly accurate. However, one room is missing here on the left-hand side where it says OC GS VRS. There was another room next to that one for the chiefs of the administration for security and of the security service. So it is between the room where it says OC GS VRS and the other one where it says VIP VO. I made a mistake, I omitted to draw that other room there as well. The rest is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the assistance of the court personnel, I would ask that you mark with an X the approximate location of that room that you have just described for us that is missing from the diagram.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here where I marked this in blue. But it was just as big as the other rooms down there. However, now it is impossible for me to draw it that big.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let the record reflect the witness has marked on the left-hand side of the document a line that appears to have two Xs interposed on top of one another above that line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not now but later I think I will and then I'll ask -- identify it first, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if so, then, of course, it's perfectly clear. The blue marking appears clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But there will be other markings and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, there will be other markings. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify for us in what space or room you performed your duties by circling that space? Again, with the assistance of the court personnel and the pen that is attached to the court monitor.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now what was the numeric designation for this room for the G-1 object, the G-1 feature?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I mark that or ... it was number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't you put a number 3 in the circle then.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist? It doesn't work at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were invited, Witness -- yes, I think the 3 is now next to the circle. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what kind of equipment was present in this room which you have marked with a circle and the number 3 where you performed your duties at the G-1 feature?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This room was for telephone equipment, multi-channel telephone equipment was kept there. RRMAV-120, VZ-4/12, and a few automatic telephones. And some M63 telephones. So it was two or three telephones of each.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now just below the room that you have marked with a circle and a 3, we see a space that has the designation ATC OM-60, and then we have two other spaces below that, PS and the other one is "Razdelnik" in B/C/S. Could you describe for us what those rooms were used for?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to mark them with numbers or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't you do that just to be on the safe side. Mark first the --

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you first then tell us about rooms -- Could you first tell us about the rooms that you've marked 1, 1A, 1B, and 1C, please? For what were those rooms used?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three smaller rooms in room 1. In PS, there is a hand-operated telephone switchboard where direct communication was established between direct telephone links and automatic telephone links. So there was an operator there who connected these telephone communications by hand. Or between automatic lines. So it was different kinds of connections that were established there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, the room that you have marked with a number 2, what was the function of that room at the G-1 feature?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell you something a moment ago. Where it says Razdelnik 1B, that is where all the cables were arriving from Veliki Zep and all the telephones. So they were all there at the distribution board, and then it was possible to switch from one channel to another. C was a generator for the automatic telephone exchange that is in room number 2. And in room number 2, there was an automatic telephone exchange, OM-60, that had 250 automatic numbers. So this was used for the direct establishment of communication through automatic telephones between two or more participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question at this moment to the witness. You are talking about automatic telephones. What is, in your understanding, an automatic telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An automatic telephone has a dial with numbers from 1 through 9. And then, for example, this was a switchboard with a three-digit number. So say you choose number 111, so you dial 1-1-1. You don't need an intermediary. You just choose the number that you want with regard to these 250 numbers. So it is similar to regular civilian PTT, the way you establish telephone communication through a telephone exchange. So it is with a dial, with numbers from 1 through 9, including 0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let me just check where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the room above the room that you've marked with a circle and a number 3, that -- the left-hand side it says teleprint ST, and the right-hand side says "prostor" [interpretation] area for repair, [In English] and then it has some letters. Could you describe for us what that room was utilized for or what those two rooms were utilized for that you've now marked with a number 4?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room number 4 where it says teleprinter station, that is where teleprinters were. RTL-1 [as interpreted] and T100 for transmitting written information via telephone channel communications equipment and radio relay after telegrams were processed, but we'll deal with that later. So that is where written information was sent from. Now, the room where it says area for repairing telephone equipment, there was a repairman there who repaired all this equipment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear any of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear what equipment was repaired in that room. Could you please repeat that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Telegraph equipment, teleprinters that were operated in room 4; that is to say, RTL-1, T100.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just above the room you've marked with a 4, there appears to be a space -- two spaces, one is a square and one is an L with the letters STPLST, and now I see you've marked it with a number 5. Could you explain for us the function of those rooms?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an encryption teleprinter station. This is a room where the encryption is and the crypto encryption, and then this other thing is a little hallway. There was nothing there. And then there were openings towards the other ones. So that is where the encryption and decryption of written information took place that was being sent to and sent from the command post of the Main Staff of the RS. I mean, information that was encrypted and sent to another side. Such telegrams that were processed were sent to room number 4 -- were handed over to room number 4 and then sent on further via teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber wonders what the -- although appreciating the details, what the relevance is of knowing exactly what teleprinters were repaired, where, in that room. So if you would first put questions to the witness which show the relevance, and then we are quite willing to look in every detail that is important for us to know in order to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can remind, Your Honours, I was responding to the request of the interpreters, so I was relaying the request of the interpreters at that point in time, not phrasing a question myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you have refrained. You have said, well, that information is not vital for the Defence and move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were these rooms that you have now marked 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, were they in use throughout the time-period that you were at G-1 during the war from 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These rooms further on. I'll mark them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please first answer the question as put to you by -- but I see now that you a have a line up, you've marked three rooms by 6, 7, and 8. But could you first now answer the question put to you by Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I marked it because they were used throughout the period from 1992 to 1995. Some of them were, some of them were not actually. That's why I marked these 6, 7, 8. They were constantly used. That is where personnel were -- I mean, the personnel who worked in rooms from 1 through 5, and the rooms on the left-hand side where it says the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, and then further down all the way down to "Staresine," that is to say, officers, they were there only from time to time; if there was an air-raid, if there was an alert. They were not busy all the time. It's not that people were in there all the time, so that's why I marked them in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just clarify in relation to rooms that you've marked 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, were those in use throughout your tenure at the G-1 feature from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for this to be marked for identification as marked, and then I'm sure between the Prosecution and I we can figure out how to get a translation for the entire diagram into English from CLSS once it becomes marked with a D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D1061.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Mr. Ivetic, do you know when this sketch or this diagram was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, just if you could tell us so that we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's either 14 or 19 November 2008, as indicated in the upper left. This was an exhibit in the Popovic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And does that mean that in the Popovic proceedings that there must have been a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, it does not mean that, Your Honours. It was without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Popovic is more lenient in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was surprised as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, on behalf of my client and the rest of the team, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this point, I finish my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Pajic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You find Ms. Hasan to your right, standing. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, you are recorded in the transcript at transcript page 28 that in room 4 was a device that is recorded as R, for Roger, TL1. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's a type of teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the microphone be adjusted, Witness, because you're now turning a bit more to the right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It's not a question of the microphone. Could the witness just speak clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also -- you're invited to speak very clearly so that the interpreters can well hear you, and could you speak slowly and then could you then repeat your answer. You were taken to transcript page 28, that in room 4 was a device that is recorded as RTL and you were asked whether that is correct. Could you repeat your answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not correct. What I said, it was a teleprinter, ETL.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now you spoke yesterday about the company for the communications garrison of the 67th Communication Regiment of the Main Staff, and you mentioned the 2nd Platoon. Now, was it made up of other platoons as well, that garrison; and if so, what were those platoons and what were they responsible for?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a company for garrison communications. There was also a platoon for telephones and telegraphs. It was used for communications at the teleprinter station and sending written information from teleprinters T100 and ETL-1. I've already mentioned that. Then the other platoon was supposed to maintain and organise communications of the automatic telephone exchange OM-60, especially the switchboards that were in number 1, and also the distribution board in the other room. And there was a radio relay platoon that was at Veliki Zep to establish radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the platoon at Veliki Zep responsible for radio relay communications?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was a squad, and I was responsible, and there were NCOs up there, and they were -- they held the rank of sergeant, these three NCOs. So there was this mixed platoon for UNF where I was commander, and that included telephone communications with frequency-carrying devices and the radio relay communications that was at Veliki Zep. So it was a squad at Veliki Zep.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now this squad of three persons that you mentioned -- is that right, there was three persons there?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, three persons were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could you name those three for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Serbula, Dragoljub Gagovic, and Lepir -- I cannot remember his first name now. Believe me. Lepir was his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And who was sitting at the switchboard in the G-1 facility in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were operators who were military conscripts. After they did their military service, they would leave, so I cannot recall all their names. So these were ordinary soldiers who were doing their military service in the signals corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The 67th Communications Regiment also comprised of two battalions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 67th Regiment consisted of two battalions, the 1st Battalion and the 2nd Battalion, then the technical support company and the garrison communications company. That is the entire 67th Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just very briefly, could you tell us what the 1st and 2nd Battalion were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion was at the location of the barracks Han Pijesak, and its task was to handle mobile communications. In case the forward command post had to be set up, the communications equipment was mounted on vehicles, and with these vehicles they would go to that command post and set up communications. So the company for garrison communications was of stationary type, and the mobile company served for mobile communications, for setting up forward command posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what about the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion exclusively served for logistics, for support to the company for garrison communications. If the chief of communications was on leave or was ill, if somebody needed to be sent to provide, among other things, security personnel for the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that -- in your platoon, the 2nd Platoon of the garrison company, you had another soldier who worked together with you. Could you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were conscripts serving their compulsory military service. They changed all the time. I can't remember now. I can't remember the names, believe me. Normal conscripts, doing their regular military service. Five or ten of them took turns.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You spoke about Vila Javor yesterday and that there was access to the underground facility G-1. Is it correct that that facility, the underground facility, is embedded in the base of Javor mountain?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the maps it was drawn as Javor, but we called it Veliki Zep. On topographic maps, it was marked as Javor, and the top of it, the summit, was called Veliki Zep. That's where the radio relay hub was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And it's at Vila Javor where General Mladic stayed; right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where he stayed. Not all the time. He had an office also in the populated area where the hutments were. It was a bit further away from Javor. He spent time also frequently at the forward command post. Part of his time he spent at Vila Javor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And at Vila Javor he had access -- I mean, he had access to a telephone?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now we spoke about the radio relay route that existed between Veliki Zep and Vlasenica, and you spoke about an unprotected line as well as a protected line. Now, where -- can you tell us where the communications station was in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications centre in Vlasenica - that is to say, the radio relay station - was at the command of the Drina Corps. It's a building belonging to the bauxite mine. At least it did before the war. I'm not quite sure about this, but I think so. That's where the communications centre was, the radio relay station.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So as far as you can recall, was the antenna then mounted on top of the Drina Corps command building?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know where exactly it was mounted. Somewhere there, whether it was on top of the building or on top of a vehicle, I'm not sure. You could mount it on a vehicle that was designated for a radio relay device or perhaps on the building. I never was interested enough to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What about at Zvornik? Do you know where the communication -- radio relay communication station was there?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, there existed a radio relay route from the communications centre at Veliki Zep to -- towards Pale; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And it was connected to Pale through Ravno Romanija and Kalovita Stena [phoen]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was protected radio relay route between the Main Staff, the president of Republika Srpska, members of the government and of the assembly, and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That's 0601 route. There was a station at Ravno Romanija and the end station at Kalovita Brda. From there, it went down by wire communications to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in Tilav and to Pale up to the Presidency and the other authorities of the Republika Srpska and in the assembly and the government, and there was also an analogue route in other directions. Unprotected ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the analogue route from Veliki Zep to Ravno Romanija, did that exist?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only 0601 route, the protected one. When I say this number, it's the designation of the route, its number. It's a digital route. And the analogue one went to the other side, across Strazbenica and Jahorina and went down to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So just so I understand it correctly, is the route - the analogue route, then - Veliki Zep-Strazbenica, Strazbenica-Pale? Were there any other nodes along that route, intermediary notes?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strazbenica-Jahorina and then Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what devices were used on this unprotected route? And if we can do it segment by segment. So between Veliki Zep and Strazbenica, what was the device that was used?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Veliki Zep-Strazbenica, the device FM-200 was used. But it worked in analogue mode, unprotected mode. I said previously this device could work in unprotected and protected modes both. It worked in analogue mode.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now from Strazbenica to Jahorina, what was the device that was used along that segment?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A device working on higher frequencies compared to FM-200. It's a device SMC-1306B. That one works in frequency range from 440.000 to 460.000 megahertz --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the other range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A different device was used with a higher frequency. V120, the multi-channel one. You couldn't uses RM4 with it. That means 12K. Its capability was 120 channels simultaneously, telephone or telegraph. It didn't matter. So it had a higher capacity compared to RRU-800, and it was difficult to intercept because it was a very large piece of equipment. It was only installed by the JNA on radio relay hubs. It could not be mounted on a vehicle because the parabolic antenna was too big. It was used only in stationary facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And are you saying that SMC-1306B was operating in analogue mode and was an unprotected line?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It worked within an analogue system with a proviso that some channels could be protected individually, like in other devices. There was no telephone device for encryption that could protect the entire system.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now how about from Jahorina to Pale?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Jahorina and Pale, FM-200 was operating with 24 channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Also operating in unprotected mode?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because it makes no sense to set up one segment protected and one segment unprotected. It makes no sense not to protect the whole channel. Analogue sections were all analogue. That means unprotected along the whole length.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now along that route, were there also RRU-800 devices?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that route, the one we're talking about now, from Jahorina to Pale that was used for those needs, as far as I know, no other device was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What about from Veliki Zep down to Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no relay route Veliki Zep-Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry. What I meant to say is between Veliki Zep through Strazbenica to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether RRU-800 was used? Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you from Veliki Zep to Strazbenica, we used FM-200. And from Jahorina to Pale, also FM-200. And the last section was SMC-1306B.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, there was a central communications centre for PTT civilian lines in Sokolac; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A civilian post office existed with civilian numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And some of those civilian lines, at least, were used by the VRS for communications; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And so there would be a phone number that you could reach the Sokolac switchboard; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And say if I was a civilian and I was calling that phone number and my call arrives in Sokolac via this PTT line and I wanted to speak to someone at the Main Staff, can you tell me how my call, along what route my call would travel to reach the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only from Sokolac from the PTT. We could do that from Pale, too. We could do it also from Han Pijesak. We had those PTT numbers. And specifically if you're ask being Sokolac, there was a radio relay route also analogue, Strazbenica-Sokolac. And using telephone and radio relay devices, we pick up the Sokolac number, never mind which, and I set it up in Crna Rijeka, I transfer it, and from there, you can dial any number in Sokolac or in Pale, anywhere. So a radio relay route was set up between Strazbenica and Sokolac. And two FM-200 devices were used, one in Sokolac, one in Strazbenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And from Strazbenica, is the route directly to Veliki Zep or is there an intermediary node between the two?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was direct. Just as the previous one. We used the radio relay route from Sokolac to Strazbenica, and then we plugged it into already existing channels from Strazbenica-Sokolac. We transferred it to Crna Rijeka, that number from Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, could I seek a clarification. You said: "And two FM-200 devices were used, one in Sokolac, one in Strazbenica." Was that operating in protected mode or unprotected note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unprotected, analogue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the -- members of the United Nations who, for example, were situated in Sarajevo, they weren't directly connected to the VRS's radio relay network, were they?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge that they were connected.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if they wanted to reach the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka, they would have call using a PTT line, at least initially?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably what they did. I really don't know. It was possible for them to do that. And along military lines, I don't know. I didn't monitor these communications. I just maintained them. I don't know whether there was a special channel for UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you know the frequency that the analogue FM-200 operated on between Veliki Zep and Strazbenica?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know off the cuff. It's probably from 610 to 960 megahertz. Within that range, you could select any frequency for transmission. And I never tried to memorize these frequencies because they were all on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So I take it then you also don't recall the frequency that operated between Strazbenica and Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't remember that. I mean, I don't remember any frequency, not only that particular one. I never needed to memorize them. It was written on the device and it was written on a separate piece of paper, so I never needed to remember them. All I know, it was within that range.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So someone from the United Nations calling from Sarajevo using a PTT line, they would dial a particular phone number that would arrive, for example, at the Sokolac PTT centre at which point their communication to the Main Staff would enter the radio relay network and be transmitted onwards?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But I have to explain. Apart from those PTT numbers from Sokolac which were at the communications centre in my headquarters, there were PTT numbers from the post office at Han Pijesak. Those telephones from the post office in Han Pijesak are connected with a special cable to Crna Rijeka. They didn't go along a radio relay route. They went along regular FM cables, and they could dial personnel from the Main Staff and they could dial personnel from the United Nations. I know for a fact that such numbers existed at the post office in Han Pijesak and the post office in Sokolac and the PTT in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So somebody calling using a PTT line dialling the Han Pijesak PTT centre would then be transmitted via cable to Crna Rijeka. It would not pass over the radio relay network; right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But when the call is coming in to Sokolac PTT -- when the call is coming in -- from Sokolac, it would enter the radio relay network to finally arrive at Crna Rijeka, if I have understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you been shown any intercepts by the Defence before you came to testify here yesterday? Intercepts that were taken by the Bosnian army or the Bosnian State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They showed me some document, but I didn't know anything about it. I had never seen them. If there were such things, it was -- they were probably submitted to the chief of communications of the Main Staff. During the war, I had never seen such documents, nor did I have any knowledge or awareness about interception.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told it's time for the break. I don't know if you want to break at this point or given that General Mladic is not in the courtroom, if we want to sit longer. I leave that in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there is a chance that Mr. Mladic would join us later, then I think it's preferable that we use our usual schedule as if he were there. So that would mean time for the break. Witness, we take a break. You may follow the usher and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to personally apologise for the late start after this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, I'm going to show you a record of an intercepted communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could take a look at P1207, and this is an under-seal exhibit so it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's intercepted by the Bosnian State Security Service. And as soon as we get the English. You can see there this is an intercept from the 11th of July, 1995, a conversation that took place at 1800 hours. And it's recorded in the header that they were monitoring the radio relay in the Pale direction on frequency 836.000 megahertz, and they recorded a conversation between General Gvero and General Gobillard. Now in this particular conversation, General Gobillard, who there's evidence is speaking from Sarajevo, could not be heard, that only one participant -- participant's voice was audible. And let's just reads the start of this -- of -- of this communication. So it's only recording what General Gvero is saying. And it starts: "General Mladic is in the field --" And I should preface this by saying you will see that it appears that is an operator speaking who then connects the call to General Gvero. It will become apparent. "General Mladic is in the field and he too is away. "I can only put him through to General Gvero if he wants. "Please. "Hold on. "Hello, this is Gvero. "Who? "Svetlana. "My regards to you and General Gobillard." Now, General Gobillard is speaking through an interpreter who we understand to be the person named here as Svetlana. So this communication, and I won't go into the contents of the rest of the conversation, is a call that's put through General Gobillard from Sarajevo through to General Gvero. Now, can you tell us, this communication would have reached a PTT centre, be it the number that Gobilliard dialled, whether it's the PTT centre in Sokolac or Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know what General Gobilliard used to call from. And this is not a complete conversation, it's just one side talking, so I don't know what the man used from where he called. There's just some frequency here, 836 megahertz, and that is within that RRU range. So the complete conversation is not there. I don't know what the man used to call. Did he call from PTT? Did he call from a direct line? I don't know. Because PTT numbers were also transferred when they were taken from the civilian PTT telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when you're talking about the civilian PTT telephone exchange, where is that located?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is Sokolac, then the post of Sokolac, if it's a civilian number. I don't know where General Gobilliard was, what the location was. So civilian PTT number from Sokolac. That was at the post office Sokolac, and then the Strazbenica-Sokolac relay equipment was also at the Sokolac post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. And it's possible that -- now, like I said, there is evidence in this case that General Gobilliard is calling from Sarajevo. So would it also have -- then be possible that he dialled the number for the Pale PTT centre to reach the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly from a Pale PTT number one can call Sokolac PTT --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did understand the rest of the sentence. Could the speaker please speak clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You started off saying that it was possible that from the Pale PTT number one can call the Sokolac PTT. So if a call comes into the Pale PTT centre, a civilian PTT line, is it not entering the radio relay network at that point on the route you spoke about before the break, the radio relay route.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if he called from a civilian PTT Pale, but he called the civilian PTT Sokolac that is at the location of Crna Rijeka and Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just make sure that I understand your evidence correctly. Are you independently saying you have knowledge that the UN call coming in from Sarajevo would have necessarily have been a call coming into the PTT Sokolac communications centre?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know about this call at all. I mean, this is the first time I'm seeing. And the second thing, I've been telling you: If from a Pale PTT number you're making a call, and if it's not part of the relay equipment, and a Sokolac number that was installed, the PTT Sokolac number was installed in Crna Rijeka, then that Sokolac number had to be in the system of the radio relay equipment and as such had to be in Crna Rijeka within this range.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the PTT centre in Pale, was that installed as -- I mean, was that a connection that existed to Crna Rijeka? I mean, what I understood you to have said, that when a call comes into Pale, that it gets into the radio relay network and travels via Jahorina-Strazbenica-Veliki Zep and then to Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If a Pale number is in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start his answer again slowly and clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you restart slowly and clearly your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that the PTT number that existed in Crna Rijeka from Sokolac, it was transferred using the system RRU FM-200 via Sokolac-Strazbenica-Crna Rijeka, so it exists in that route. And man who calls from Pale from a telephone exchange, civilian exchange, then he calls that number, it can be listened to at the Sokolac-Strazbenica-Veliki Zep route. I mean, that conversation can be heard. I mean, we've already said what is needed for intercepting that conversation. So let me explain this for you: Military equipment, radio relay equipment, could have heard this call only within Sokolac-Strazbenica-Veliki Zep because the Sokolac number that arrived in Veliki Zep takes that route. I don't know if I've explained it to you. I don't know how else to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it this is an answer to your question, Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So then this communication was travelling on an open line to Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Veliki Zep radio relay system, and then it went down by cable to Crna Rijeka; that is to say, it is an analogue relay throughout was not protected. I've already said that individual channels can be protected. Individual ones, not all of them. So, say, from 12 to 24. In this case, I think it was 24 channels - in this case - not all of them could have been protected individually or they were, if necessary. And in order to listen in to an analogue unprotected conversation, I've already explained what was needed in my previous answer, and I have no knowledge of interception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you tend to repeat things you had said before. There's no need for that. I think the beginning of your answer was clear, that it was a -- it travelled through an unprotected radio relay system where only individual channels could be protected. That's, in short, what I understood to be your answer. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
